title: Polylogarithmic communication for two-server private information retrieval

importance.reason: A longstanding gap in the unconditional communication cost of private database access, even with only two noncommunicating servers and no computational hardness assumption.

category_assignment.reason: A fundamental limit on information-theoretic security or generic cryptanalysis, rather than a construction from an assumed primitive.

notes: Adopts the classical one-round perfect-privacy and zero-error model in Dvir–Gopi Definition 1.1; polylogarithmic target is explicitly discussed in the 2026 primary source.
Makes the communication-only, nonuniform convention explicit; no extra efficient-server or single-bit-answer condition is imposed.
The year records the dated model and problem source, not the first introduction of PIR.
Deduplicated against active TCS-7459, TCS-2732 and TCS-1020; these concern different resources or tasks.

import_provenance.purpose: User-requested major cryptography problems outside primitive-construction implications. New candidates are red.

formal:
Private information retrieval lets a user recover a selected database bit without revealing its index to either server. Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), a classical one-round two-server protocol with perfect correctness and perfect privacy has total communication at most
\[
C(\log_2 n)^k
\]
bits for every database \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), requested index \(i\in[n]\), and outcome of the user's randomness? The two servers each hold the entire database and do not communicate or collude. Model & notation specifies the protocol and exact privacy requirement. There is no computational hardness assumption or bound on local computation.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(n\), a protocol specifies a nonempty finite randomness set \(\mathcal R_n\), query maps \(Q_{1,n},Q_{2,n}\), deterministic answer maps \(A_{1,n},A_{2,n}\), and a deterministic recovery map \(D_n\). Queries and answers are finite binary strings. The user samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\mathcal R_n\), independently of the database, and sends \(q_j=Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) to server \(j\). The server sends back \(a_j=A_{j,n}(x,q_j)\). There is one query and one answer per server. The user starts with only \(n,i,r\), with no database-dependent advice or shared secret.

Perfect correctness means \(D_n(i,r,a_1,a_2)=x_i\) for every \(x,i,r\). Perfect privacy means that for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and all \(i,i'\in[n]\), the random strings \(Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) and \(Q_{j,n}(i',r)\) have identical distributions. Since answers are deterministic functions of a server's database and query, this also protects its entire view. The servers follow the protocol; robustness to false answers and confidentiality of the rest of the database from the user are not required.

The cost is the maximum of \(|q_1|+|q_2|+|a_1|+|a_2|\) over all \(x,i,r\), where \(|w|\) is the bit length of a string \(w\). Protocol descriptions may depend on \(n\) but not on \(x\) or \(i\). There is no uniformity or local-running-time restriction. The same constants \(C,k\) must work for every database size; they cannot grow with \(n\). Answers may contain more than one bit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a protocol family and universal constants exist, or prove the logical negation. Privacy must be exact against each computationally unbounded individual server. The bound includes both queries and both answers in the worst case. Computational privacy, database-dependent client preprocessing, or a growing number of servers changes the target.
why: Can keeping the address of a requested bit completely secret cost only a polynomial in the address length? This isolates the information cost of privacy from encryption assumptions, server computation and implementation details.

context_blocks.text: With one server, perfect private retrieval of an arbitrary bit requires sending the whole database in the standard model. Two noncommunicating copies permit much smaller communication. The user can correlate the two queries while each query separately hides the requested index.

Dvir and Gopi give a one-round protocol with communication \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n}))\). This grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\), but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their Definition 1.1 supplies the exact correctness and privacy model used here.

Ghasemi and Kopparty explicitly identify polylogarithmic two-server communication as consistent with known lower bounds in their ITCS 2026 paper. Their lower bounds constrain a particular algebraic framework, not all protocols.

The October 2026 revision of Gupte and Ragavan improves communication for several fixed server counts. Its displayed bound at two servers still has the square-root logarithmic exponent above and does not reach the present polylogarithmic target.

TCS-7459 instead concerns computational privacy at a single server and the cost of preprocessing and answering queries. These are different models and objectives; neither card is merely a parameter change in the other.

progress.text: Dvir and Gopi obtain \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n}))\) communication with two servers.
Ghasemi and Kopparty explicitly state that polylogarithmic communication with two servers remains possible given known bounds.
Gupte and Ragavan revise their improvement for several fixed server counts; the two-server specialization remains above polylogarithmic communication.

status_note: Targeted literature check on 6 November 2026 found no matching protocol or impossibility theorem. The October 2026 fewer-server result was checked separately. Computational PIR and protocols with client preprocessing do not resolve this unconditional, fresh-client model.

sentences: A user wants one bit from a database replicated at two servers that do not communicate.
Each individual server must learn nothing about which bit was requested.
The question asks whether one round can use only a fixed power of the logarithm of the database size in total bits.
Correctness and privacy are perfect, while local computation is unrestricted.
The known subpolynomial protocols leave a substantial gap to this communication target.
